title: Shishupala
hook: a light rises from the fallen king and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira finishes his rite
carry: where you'd rather turn that light

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shishupala used up his hundred pardons, and Krishna spoke, then acted. Your line was name your limit, kindly and clearly. Did you name a limit to yourself, kindly and clearly? Day seven hundred sixty-three.
screen: `PATIENCE WITH A SHAPE AND A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Shishupala has fallen, and the hall is silent. But the poem isn't done with him. Something rises from his body: a radiance, the text says, bright as the sun. Every eye in the hall follows it. It moves toward Krishna, bows to him, and enters him. The man who railed against Krishna in front of every king ends inside him. It's a strange ending, and the poem says the kings who saw it were amazed. Today, the light, the funeral, and the end of the Rajasuya.
screen: `A LIGHT RISES FROM HIS BODY.` → `IT BOWS TO KRISHNA.` → `IT ENTERS HIM.`

segments.voice: What does it mean that Shishupala's light enters Krishna? The poem shows it and moves on, so readers have filled the space. Some Hindus, especially in devotional traditions, read it this way: Shishupala thought about Krishna constantly, even if every thought was hatred, and that fierce, single-minded attention brought him to Krishna in the end. Others read it more simply: everything that lives returns, at last, to its source. The text doesn't settle it, and neither will we. Then the story turns practical. Yudhishthira, the host, does what a just king does after a death in his hall. He has the funeral rites performed for Shishupala, and he places Shishupala's son on the throne of Chedi. The fallen king's line keeps its crown. The rite is finished, the guests are honored and sent home, and Krishna returns to his own city. Now look back at the week. We started at the Rajasuya, with everyone handed a job, Krishna washing feet and Duryodhana receiving the gifts. Bhishma named Krishna for the first honor, and Shishupala stood up. He made his case, and Yudhishthira answered with gentleness. The kings grew angry, Bhishma spoke of a sleeping lion, and held Bhima back. Then the cradle, and a promise of a hundred pardons. Then the limit, and the discus. And now the light. Shishupala's story ends here. But remember the cousin at the gift table. He's still in Indraprastha, and the next story is his.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE LIGHT MEAN?` · `THE FUNERAL, AND A NEW KING.` · `THE RITE IS FINISHED.` · `LOOKING BACK AT THE WEEK.` · then, large: `THE COUSIN AT THE GIFT TABLE.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let this be a resting sit after a heavy week. Bring to mind someone you've had real trouble with, someone who takes up a lot of room in your thoughts. Notice how much attention you've given them. You don't have to change how you feel. Just see the attention itself, as if it were a light you've been shining at them. Breathe in, and gather it back a little. Breathe out, and let it rest. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer for a moment. If not, simply let your attention come home. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. Krishna's cousin and fierce opponent, pardoned a hundred times, whose light rose at the end and entered Krishna.
Your line: where you'd rather turn that light. Today, notice who takes up the most room in your thoughts, and where you'd rather turn that light. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: In some devotional traditions, the end of Shishupala is told as a teaching that even hatred, if it fixes the mind on Krishna, can bring a person to him; other readers take a different meaning, and the Mahabharata itself does not explain the light.

it shows the light entering Krishna and moves on; readers differ on its meaning.
the light rose into the sky and vanished
the poem says it bowed to Krishna and entered him.
the Rajasuya was completed after Shishupala's death

fork.setup: you're one of the kings in the hall. Shishupala has fallen, and a light rises from his body. where does it go?
fork.reveal: the poem says the light bowed to Krishna and entered him, and the kings were amazed. it shows this without explaining it.

original.note: Sanskrit tejas: radiance, brilliant energy; a light like this rises from Shishupala and enters Krishna.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story ends when Shishupala dies.
what it means: a light rises from him and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira gives him a funeral and crowns his son.
what a scholar hears: the text shows the light without explaining it, and later devotional readers took it as a teaching about the power of a mind fixed on Krishna.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sisupala-badha Parva (the radiance rising from Shishupala's body and entering Krishna; funeral rites; Shishupala's son installed; the Rajasuya completed)
Bhagavata Purana, Book 7, chapter 1 (the teaching that fixing the mind on the Lord, even in enmity, leads to him, with Shishupala as an example)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the radiance rising from Shishupala's body, bowing to Krishna and entering him, and the kings' amazement.
Confirm Yudhishthira orders the funeral rites and installs Shishupala's son as king of Chedi.

The devotional reading (attention fixed on Krishna even in hatred) is attributed to 'some Hindus, especially in devotional traditions'; the Bhagavata Purana reference for it should be checked by a Keeper.
Original: tejas is offered as a gloss for the radiance; confirm it is the word in the Sanskrit at this point, or set original to null.
Editor pass: cut 'spent his whole life railing against Krishna' (a claim about his whole life the cited scene doesn't make) and kept it to what he did in the hall.

Audit (2026-10-01): the fork (take the kingdom or crown the son?) and the myth about seizing Chedi repeated day 755's Magadha fork and myth almost exactly; replaced both with items about the light, and trimmed the teach's matching 'no taking the kingdom' line. Fixed the garbled 'offer that person into your prayer'.
